Parked and Dismantled: 1970 Plymouth Cuda Flaunts Ultra-Rare Features
16 photos
Photo: eBay/Duffy's Classic Cars
After six years in production, the Plymouth Barracuda changed platforms in 1970, adopting Chrysler's then-new E-body underpinnings. The swap also brought a sportier-looking Barracuda into dealerships, as well as high-compression big-block V8 engines on the options list.
The restyled Mopar proved popular, selling nearly 49,000 examples. About a third of these cars were ordered in the performance-oriented Cuda trim, the only one available with the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi and the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB. The latter came in two flavors, with a four-barrel carburetor and a 3x2 setup (six-barrel).
Only 3,436 units were ordered with these three powerplants, which are now the most desirable on the classic car market. Exactly 986 were equipped with the four-barrel 440, 1,784 were fitted with the six-barrel 440, while 666 got the Hemi V8. But it's not just engines that can make a 1970 Barracuda rare. The convertible top is also a rare sight.
That's because only 2,501 customers opted to have a retractable roof (that's only 5.1% of the total production). Mind you, this number includes all three models: the Barracuda, Gran Coupe , and Cuda. Base model sales included 1,387 examples, while the Gran Coupe convertible moved 566 units. The remaining 548 cars were ordered as high-performance Cudas.
The latter came with a choice of five powerplants. In addition to the aforementioned 440 and Hemi, customers could also get a 340-cubic-inch (5.6-liter) small-block V8 marketed as a fuel-efficient performance option. The drop-top came standard with the 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) big-block V8.
The Hemi is obviously the rarest, with just 14 units made. The Six-Barrel comes next with 29 examples, while the four-barrel 440 was fitted into 34 cars. Exactly 206 buyers went with the standard 383 V8, while the other 262 customers opted for the 340 V8. All told, the Cuda convertible is rare regardless of what's under the hood.
If you haven't seen one in a while, one popped up for sale in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. It's in pretty bad shape as is, but it comes with plenty of parts to start the restoration , and, more importantly, it has a very low production number.
No, this Cuda is not a Hemi Mopar, but it boasts a two-digit production figure thanks to its drivetrain combo. It's one of the 206 cars sold with the standard 383-cubic-inch V8, but it has a manual transmission. The four-speed narrows the production number to only 68 units. Moreover, it has air conditioning, which is super rare on a drop top (specific numbers are unknown).
The Cuda was born in EV2 Hemi Orange , but the high-impact color is only visible on a few components. Most body panels are either covered in surface rust or primer. As I said, the seller is selling the vehicle in a very early restoration phase. But there's plenty of good news to run by.
For starters, the Cuda still has the numbers-matching engine and transmission. That's great news for when the car will be nice and shiny (think a six-figure value). Second, the seller has already gathered the part required for the restoration, including many brand-new body panels.
Much of the car has already been dismantled, so this Cuda is ready to go into the shop. But you'll have to win the eBay auction to make it yours. Bidding has reached $35,000 with about five days to go, and the reserve hasn't been met. How much is this project car worth?
